stories.title: Nobody likes data centers and chips, chips, chips
stories.summary: Hope everyone's autumn is off to a chilly good start. This is Yifan, sending this week's techAsia from Silicon Valley.
stories.content:
Hope everyone's autumn is off to a chilly good start. This is Yifan, sending this week's #techAsia from Silicon Valley.

I just came back from a reporting trip to Indiana where I got to preview SK Hynix's first advanced chip packaging plant in the U.S., which will come online in late 2028 and assemble highly sought-after high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.

I've visited a fair amount of plants and construction sites in recent years to document America's effort to reshore manufacturing, but I was still surprised when I saw how close the SK Hynix chip plant is to the townhouses and apartments right across the street.

While local residents have protested and even sued the South Korean memory chip giant for putting this massive chip facility near residential areas, SK Hynix said the noise and pollution from such an advanced manufacturing site will be minimal, while the economic benefits will be huge, with 7,000 jobs created in the area.

As Washington is determined to bring manufacturing, especially semiconductor production, back to America, local communities like the one in Indiana are caught in the conundrum of having more job opportunities but bearing the environmental cost of such projects.

While the energy consumption of artificial intelligence data centers and its impact on the environment have been making headlines for months, the environmental cost of manufacturing AI chips and servers is also too substantial to dismiss.

So far, Asia is bearing most of those costs, as chip manufacturing is heavily concentrated in the region. Now it's time for the U.S. to rise to the challenge of balancing a growing semiconductor industry with keeping a clean and sustainable homeland for generations to come.

## Not in my backyard

Data center development across the Asia-Pacific has gathered pace since the 2010s, driven by cloud computing and video streaming. Artificial intelligence is adding another wave of demand. The region's data center demand stood at 28 gigawatts in 2025, or one-third of the global total -- behind North America at 43% -- with capacity expected to triple by 2030, according to consultancy McKinsey & Co.

But unease over data centers and related infrastructure is also growing in the region as residents push back on such projects over concerns about rising electricity prices and potential pollution, Nikkei Asia's **Tsubasa Suruga**, **Shaun Turton** and **Ananta Agarwal** report.

In Moss Vale, a small Australian town surrounded by rolling farmland about halfway between Sydney and Canberra, opposition to a gas-fired power plant intended to support data centers began in a WhatsApp chat group for preschool parents.

Such grassroots movements against data centers can be seen across the Asia-Pacific and the U.S., providing increasing examples of how local opposition is prompting developers to pull back on projects or officials to make regulatory changes.

## Dramatic changes

Chinese actors and online influencers have a new rival: cost-effective advanced AI video generation programs that are threatening millions of jobs in a once-vibrant area of China's gig economy, write the Financial Times' **Joe Leahy** and **Isaac Castella-McDonald**.

The release of powerful new AI-powered video software, such as tech group ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 model, has allowed digital actors to replace humans, enabling the production of higher-quality original videos more quickly.

The digital takeover intensified after this year's release of Seedance 2.0, said Greg Wollner, a short-drama actor and producer in Beijing. Before its release, he was shooting three different productions a week. "And after that, everything just went." Many of Wollner's friends "had to quit doing what they love and change to something else," he said.

In May, 89 of the top 100 animated dramas on Douyin, ByteDance's domestic Chinese version of TikTok, were AI productions, according to DataEye, a marketing analytics company.

In the first quarter of 2026, about 128,000 short dramas were released in China, more than three times the entire previous year and 95% of them were AI generated, according to the China Netcasting Services Association.

The economic consequences could be dramatic. China's short-drama industry employs 690,000 people directly, according to a 2026 report from the National School of Development at Peking University. About 15 million people cite live streaming as their primary profession, according to a 2024 report from the China Netcasting Services Association.

## Faster and faster

Google is accelerating its schedule for developing and rolling out its own customized chips, shifting from a two-year cycle for each generation to introducing two chips a year and eventually even more to stay ahead in the artificial intelligence race, Nikkei Asia's **Cheng Ting-Fang** and **Lauly Li** report.

"We at Google went from releasing a TPU every two years or so to one TPU a year and to this past year, two TPUs a year," Amin Vahdat, the company's chief technologist and senior vice president for AI infrastructure, said during an opening keynote at the Semicon Taiwan industry show this week.

TPUs, or tensor processing units, are Google's own AI computing chips, performing AI-related tasks similar to what Nvidia's GPUs, or graphics processing units, do. The accelerated product roadmap comes as capital expenditure for AI infrastructure surges across the industry, with Google itself planning to spend up to $205 billion to build out AI capacity this year.

The latest generation includes the TPU 8t and TPU 8i, the first one for training AI models and the second for inference. Both were introduced this year. Google debuted its first TPU in 2015.

## No downturn in sight

The chief of South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix said the global memory chip shortage is expected to last until the end of 2030 and oversupply risk is low as memory chips are no longer "just commodities" in the AI era.

The memory chip giant officially broke ground in the state of Indiana last week on its first U.S. advanced chip packaging plant, which aims to start volume production of next-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips in the second half of 2029.

SK Hynix and other leading memory chipmakers have been racing to ramp up capacity, but the global shortage is expected to continue to the end of 2030, CEO Kwak Noh-Jung told Nikkei Asia's **Yifan Yu** during a media briefing.

Despite concerns around a potential bubble in AI investment, Kwak said he sees "no signal" for oversupply risk or a memory chip downturn to come as demand from AI customers remains strong.

While memory chips used to be commodity-like, products such as HBM require more customization to tailor them to the specific needs of customers in the AI era, thus "we can more easily forecast the demand from the market," Kwak said.

stories.title: Amazon signs first APAC battery storage tolling deal with Anza Power in Victoria, Australia
stories.summary: Tied to the Bairnsdale Battery Energy Storage System in Victoria, Australia
stories.content:
Amazon has signed a battery energy storage tolling deal with Anza Power to support the development of the 50MW/200MWh Bairnsdale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in East Gippsland, Victoria, Australia.

The deal is Amazon’s first standalone battery storage tolling agreement in the APAC market. A tolling agreement is a contract in which a BESS asset is leased to a third party in exchange for a fixed, guaranteed periodic payment.

The project will connect directly to the grid as a standalone asset to provide dedicated storage capacity independent of a renewable asset. According to the companies, the agreement will help strengthen regional grid reliability and energy flexibility, enabling electricity to be stored and dispatched during periods of peak demand.

Anza has not disclosed when it expects the project to become operational.

“Signing Amazon’s first standalone battery storage tolling agreement is an important milestone for Anza Power and reflects the growing demand from major energy purchasers for dedicated storage solutions that support a reliable, low-carbon grid,” said Carlo Frigerio, CEO of Anza. “Bairnsdale demonstrates our ability to deliver flexible energy infrastructure that responds to the evolving needs of both the market and our customers. We look forward to building on the momentum we have established since launching Anza earlier this year.”

The deal builds on an existing relationship between the two companies. In April, the two firms inked five solar-plus-battery storage Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with Anza, as part of nine deals it announced in Australia for approximately 430MW of power.

Anza was launched in January by global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital as part of its ISQ Growth Markets Infrastructure Fund II. Outside of the Amazon deal, Anza also signed a virtual PPA with Fonterra in June tied to a 42MW solar farm in New Zealand.

While the deal is Amazon’s first standalone battery storage offtake agreement, it has previously acquired battery assets to support its data center portfolio. For example, in January, the firm acquired a shovel-ready solar-plus-storage facility in Morrow County, Oregon.

stories.title: Keppel acquires majority stake in two Tokyo data centers
stories.summary: Keppel has acquired a controlling stake in two Tokyo data centers, expanding its footprint in Japan's capital. The identity of the seller and the financial terms of the transaction have not been made public.
stories.why_it_matters: The deal underscores continued institutional appetite for Tokyo data center assets even as land and power constraints tighten, and it strengthens Keppel's position against rival platforms competing for Japanese hyperscale and enterprise demand. For the market, undisclosed pricing makes it harder to benchmark valuations in one of APAC's most closely watched metros.

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
Singapore’s Keppel is acquiring a majority stake in two data centers in Tokyo, Japan.

Keppel DC REIT and Keppel Ltd. this week announced that they have indirectly entered into agreements with unrelated third-party sellers to collectively acquire 90 percent effective interests in facilities now known as Tokyo Data Centre 4 and Tokyo Data Centre 5, two freehold, hyperscale fully-fitted (colocation) facilities located in Inzai City.

![keppel dc 4 and 5 tokyo](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/keppel_dc_4_and_5_tokyo.width-358.png) 

The deal (on a 100 percent basis) is valued at JPY 190 billion ($1.197bn).

Upon completion, Keppel DC REIT will hold an 88.62 percent effective interest in each facility. Keppel Ltd., through its interest in Keppel Japan KK, will hold a 1.38 percent effective interest.

The existing operator, an unnamed “established global data center owner and operator,” will retain a 10 percent interest in each data center.

The deals will be largely funded via funds from a new private placement.

Tokyo Data Centre 4 and Tokyo Data Centre 5 total a gross floor area of 169,590 sq ft (15,755 sqm) and 233,550 sq ft (21,698 sqm) respectively, with an approximate net lettable area of 62,135 sq ft (5,773 sqm) and 101,160 sq ft (9,398 sqm) respectively. Tokyo 4 was completed in 2021, Tokyo 5 in 2024.

Both fully occupied, the weighted average lease expiry (WALE) is approximately 4.5 years for Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 10.6 years for Tokyo Data Centre 5. Of the four investment-grade clients across the two data centers (three in building 4 and two in building 5), three are new to Keppel DC REIT’s portfolio

Loh Hwee Long, CEO of the manager of Keppel DC REIT, said: “This acquisition demonstrates our disciplined approach to acquiring quality assets with multiple avenues for value creation. In addition to immediate DPU accretion, Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5 provide embedded growth through contracted rent escalators and meaningful potential reversion opportunities, while further deepening our exposure to the Japan data center market.

"The acquisition also expands our network of institutional and operating partners, strengthening our ability to source and access future investment opportunities globally. Together, these will support our strategy of building a resilient portfolio that can deliver sustainable long-term growth and returns across market cycles.”

This week also saw Keppel DC REIT announce the successful completion of a new private placement, which was upsized to S$625 million (US$492.76m) from S$600 million (US$472.05m).

Approximately S$615.8 million (US$485.51m) will go towards partially financing the acquisition. The rest will go towards fees and general corporate and/or working capital purposes.

DBS Bank Ltd., Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited, Jefferies Singapore Limited, and United Overseas Bank Limited were the joint bookrunners and underwriters for the Private Placement.

Keppel DC REIT was listed on the Singapore Exchange in December 2014 as the first pure-play data center REIT in Asia. The company is managed by Keppel DC REIT Management Pte. Ltd. and sponsored by Keppel.

The company’s portfolio comprises a mix of fully-fitted (colocation/single tenant) and shell and core facilities across Singapore, Australia, China, Japan, Malaysia, Germany, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, and the UK.

The company currently owns two other data centers in Tokyo; Tokyo Data Centre 1 and Tokyo Data Centre 3. The latter was acquired last year.

The Inzai area of Tokyo is one of the city's data center hotspots. Operators including STT GDC, Airtrunk, Digital Realty, and Colt have a presence in the region.

stories.title: Ada Infrastructure breaks ground on latest Tokyo data center
stories.summary: Ada Infrastructure has started construction on a new data center in Tokyo, adding to its development pipeline in Japan. The company has not disclosed construction timelines or the facility's capacity.
stories.why_it_matters: Another groundbreaking in Tokyo confirms that developers remain willing to commit capital despite the city's acute power and land constraints. The lack of disclosed specifications, however, keeps analysts guessing about the project's scale and target customers in an increasingly crowded market.
stories.content:
Data center firm Ada Infrastructure has started work on another new data center in Tokyo.

![Ada tokyo groundbreak august 2026](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/1788218876700.width-358.jpg) 

“Last week, we held the groundbreaking ceremony for our fifth project in Japan, as well as the third and final building at Tokyo's TKW1 campus,” Ada announced on LinkedIn this week.

Ada broke ground on the first building at the TKW1 campus in August 2023. Work on the second began in May 2024. The campus will total two 10MW buildings and one 11MW facility. The first was due to go live in May 2025; the second is due to go live in 2027.

“Our third groundbreaking ceremony, second in Tokyo in just four months. Ada is truly moving at an unprecedented pace,” said Ras Scollay, principal, revenue and product lead, APAC at Ada Infrastructure.

Ada was founded by Singapore-based logistics-focused real estate firm GLP in 2023 to develop and hold the firm’s non-Chinese data center assets. Ada and GLP’s other international assets were acquired by Ares in 2024.

The firm previously outlined plans to invest ~$12 billion over five years to deliver 900MW of data center capacity in Japan. The company currently has plans to build five campuses totaling 600MW; four in Tokyo (TKW1, TKW2, TKE1, and TKE2) and one in Osaka.

Tokyo West 2 will offer 295MW across eight five-story buildings by 2026; Tokyo East 1 will offer 66MW across three four-story buildings by 2026; and Tokyo East 2 will offer 190MW across four four-story buildings from 2027.

Ada also has projects in development in the UK and Brazil.

stories.title: Vertiv acquires microgrid company UtilityInnovation
stories.summary: Sees data center supplier move up the chain into the behind-the-meter space
stories.content:
Data center power and cooling company Vertiv is to acquire microgrid firm UtilityInnovation.

NYSE-listed Vertiv Holdings this week announced that its wholly owned subsidiary, Vertiv Corporation, has entered into an agreement and plan of merger to acquire Utility Innovation Holdings, Inc., which operates as UtilityInnovation Group (UIG).

![utilityinnovation group](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/utilityinnovation_group.width-358.png) 

The deal is for approximately $1.45 billion in cash at closing, with additional consideration of up to $1.15 billion in cash based on achieving certain financial targets over 12- and 24-month periods. The transaction is expected to close later this year.

Founded in 2020 and based in Raleigh, North Carolina, UIG designs and delivers power systems that support real-time load and frequency balancing across behind-the-meter systems and utility-connected energy resources. Its solutions include proprietary controls software, customized microgrid switchgear and energy storage. Volvo Penta previously invested in the company.

Vertiv said the acquisition will see the company move upstream to the grid interconnect, adding microgrid controls, on-site generation and energy storage orchestration, and behind-the-meter power architecture to help data center operators secure power faster amid ongoing grid constraints.

“For AI data center operators, competitive advantage increasingly depends on how quickly they can move from site selection to first token,” said Gio Albertazzi, Vertiv CEO. “Vertiv has the most complete power and cooling portfolio in the industry. With UIG, we anticipate extending that portfolio upstream to the utility interconnect and onsite power sources, creating a coordinated architecture from source to chip without tying customers to a single generation technology or supplier.”

Albertazzi continued: “Together, we anticipate being better positioned to support grid-connected sites, bridge-to-grid deployments and islanded sites supplied by onsite generation, while reducing complexity from site planning through rack-level deployment. This broader capability can help customers accelerate time to power and, ultimately, time to first token.”

One of the major players in the data center supply chain, Vertiv has been busy on the M&A front. 2026 has seen the company acquire data center cooling firm ThermoKey, prefab enclosure maker Bmarko, and coldplate specialist Strategic Thermal Labs.

UIG founder and CEO Sidney Hinton added: “UIG was founded to solve increasingly complex power challenges for data center operators through flexible, technology-agnostic architectures. Vertiv’s global scale, critical infrastructure portfolio and service capabilities make it a strong strategic fit for what we have built. We believe this combination can expand the reach of UIG’s microgrid controls and power architecture expertise and create greater value for customers as power becomes an increasingly critical constraint on data center growth.”

Hinton previously founded PowerSecure, a provider of utility and energy technologies that was bought out in 2016 by Southern Company for $431 million.

UtilityInnovation last year partnered with EPC Power Corp. to launch a new power system offering engineered for AI data centers.

J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is acting as financial advisor to Vertiv, and Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney PC is serving as legal counsel. Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC is acting as financial advisor to UIG, and Davis Polk & Wardwell LLP is serving as legal counsel.

With the boom in liquid cooling to support AI workloads, Vertiv has acquired a number of businesses to bolster its offering.

In 2023, the company acquired coolant distribution infrastructure provider CoolTera. The next year, it picked up centrifugal chiller technology and assets from BiXin Energy Technology Co.

Last year, it bought automation platform WayLay.io, which develops monitoring and control technologies for power and cooling systems. It also acquired rack maker Great Lakes for $200m and mechanical flushing firm PurgeRite.

stories.title: Four out of six subsea cables in Vietnam out of service
stories.summary: Four out of six subsea cables connecting Vietnam with the rest of Asia are out of service after developing issues over the past few months, according to local reports. This has caused widespread internet disruptions across the country although these have been alleviated by backup infrastructure. Vietnam is linked by six subsea fiber-optic cable systems […]
stories.content:
Four out of six subsea cables connecting Vietnam with the rest of Asia are out of service after developing issues over the past few months, according to local reports. This has caused widespread internet disruptions across the country although these have been alleviated by backup infrastructure.

Vietnam is linked by six subsea fiber-optic cable systems – AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC and SJC2. Since 2022, Vietnam has experienced an average of 10 incidents a year, according to local reports. Repairs can take several months up to a year.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/MYCDC-Malaysia-1024x199.jpg)

The latest disruption occurred last week affecting the SJC2 cable which connects Vietnam to other parts of Asia. A segment near Hong Kong has developed a fault.

Since February, the AAE-1 cable has been out of service and has yet to be repaired.

The Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the U.S., and the Intra Asia (IA) cable are also experiencing issues, with repairs expected to start early September.

Local internet service providers have been balancing loads, rerouting traffic and adding capacity through other connections to minimize the downtime. Vietnam’s international internet traffic is mostly routed through subsea fiber-optic cables.

However, internet services generally remain stable as they are supported by backup infrastructure, according to network provider VNPT. It would only be “somewhat affected” during peak hours, it reportedly said.

Viettel meanwhile reportedly said it has added 800 Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable last week, as well as 300 Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway. It has also rerouted some international traffic through a terrestrial cable running via Laos to Singapore, and plans to add another 1.5 Tbps of capacity on that route.

Viettel added it could increase capacity on its Asia Direct Cable (ADC) to 50 Tbps, if needed, to “handle all international Internet traffic.” The new ADC links Vietnam with Hong Kong, Singapore, and Japan.

![](https://w.media/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Issue-13-Banner-1-1024x201.jpg)

Last year, Vietnam launched its first VSTN terrestrial fiber optic cable and has approved trials of satellite internet services. In August, it licensed Elon Musk’s Starlink to provide satellite internet services in Vietnam, becoming the first company to do so. The government hopes these measures would reduce its dependence on subsea cables and help alleviate the frequent disruptions.

stories.title: Semiconductor Equipment Market to Hit $344 Billion by 2032
stories.summary: The global semiconductor manufacturing equipment market is projected to reach USD 344.36 billion by 2032, driven by the increasing demand for advanced chips for artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) applications. This growth is directly linked to the expansion of data centers and the need for sophisticated tools to produce advanced-node semiconductors.
stories.content:
### Market Dynamics and Drivers

Semiconductor manufacturing equipment encompasses specialised tools and systems used across the entire chip production lifecycle, from front-end wafer fabrication processes such as lithography, etching, and deposition, to back-end processes including assembly, packaging, and testing. These tools ensure the nanometer-scale precision required for high-performance chips.A primary driver for market growth is the ongoing trend towards miniaturisation and the adoption of advanced manufacturing processes. Smaller transistor geometries offer higher performance, reduced power consumption, and increased functional density, benefits highly valued by cloud data center operators and automotive manufacturers.Analysts also identify advanced packaging technologies, including system-in-package (SiP), fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP), and 3D stacking, as a major opportunity. These innovations are critical for enhancing performance, thermal management, and integration density as semiconductor devices continue to shrink and become more power-efficient.

### Regional Trends and Challenges

Asia Pacific dominated the global semiconductor manufacturing equipment market in 2024, holding an 81% share, reflecting the region's strong position in fabrication capacity across countries like China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.The Americas is expected to be the fastest-growing region during the forecast period. This growth is spurred by substantial government incentives, such as the US CHIPS and Science Act, which provides extensive funding to boost domestic chip production and research and development (R&D) activities. This has led to significant investments in new fabrication facilities and technology clusters across various states. The push for supply chain resilience and nearshoring of manufacturing, coupled with growth in advanced applications like AI and automotive, further drives demand in the region.Despite strong growth projections, high ownership and operational costs remain a significant restraint. Cutting-edge tools, such as extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, can cost over USD 200 million per unit. Such capital intensity limits leading-edge equipment access to only a small group of well-capitalised foundries and integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), potentially slowing fab-capacity expansion.

### India's Context

India's expanding digital infrastructure and ambitions in AI will increasingly rely on access to advanced semiconductors and the sophisticated equipment required to produce them. Global trends in domestic chip production and the rising cost of manufacturing technology will influence investment decisions for advanced data center technologies and supply chain resilience within India.

stories.title: AI Drives Data Center Fire Risk, Demanding New Protection Strategies
stories.summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is increasing power density in data centers, introducing new fire risks that traditional protection methods may not adequately address. This necessitates an integrated design approach considering advanced electrical and cooling technologies for enhanced operational resilience.
stories.content:
### Higher Power Density Concerns

AI infrastructure growth is significantly increasing the power delivered to individual equipment racks. While many data centers operate at lower densities, some high-performance systems now exceed 40 kW per rack, with newer AI installations potentially surpassing 100 kW per rack.Higher rack density itself does not inherently increase fire likelihood, but concentrating more power and heat in smaller areas alters how fire risks should be evaluated. Potential concerns include overloaded electrical equipment, damaged connections, insulation failures, and cooling interruptions. This underscores the importance of early coordination, with fire protection engineers involved from the initial design stages. Airflow patterns must be considered for detection device placement, especially in areas with high air movement, and sprinkler and suppression system layouts must account for potential obstructions.

### New Technologies Introduce Risks

Lithium-ion batteries are increasingly used in uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems due to their space efficiency and performance characteristics, but they introduce fire protection concerns such as thermal runaway, combustible gas production, fire propagation, and potential for reignition. Installations require specific consideration beyond traditional battery room approaches, with engineers needing to understand project-specific battery systems and their influence on overall fire protection strategy. Installation requirements depend on whether the battery system is part of a UPS (UL 1778) or classified as a stationary energy storage system (UL 9540), with UL 9540A providing a test method for thermal runaway fire propagation.Cooling technologies are also evolving, with data center designers considering direct-to-chip liquid cooling and immersion cooling for high-density computing. These methods introduce new fire protection considerations related to cooling fluid properties and potential leaks near energised equipment. Changes in airflow may also affect the detection speed of traditional smoke detection systems. The appropriate protection strategy should be based on the specific hazards associated with the technology being used, rather than simply adding more systems.

### Lessons from Real-World Incidents

A 2021 fire at a data center campus in Strasbourg, France, highlighted critical lessons. A French government investigation identified an electrical fault involving a UPS and connected batteries as the origin. The affected building had fire detection but lacked an automatic extinguishing system. Investigators also concluded that building construction and proximity of nearby structures contributed to the fire's spread. The incident destroyed one data center and disrupted operations across the campus, demonstrating that containing an event depends on more than just equipment-level protection.For owners and operators, this incident underscores that resilience extends beyond code compliance. Fire protection planning must consider emergency procedures, system commissioning, impairment planning, coordinated shutdown procedures, and emergency response training and drills. While data centers are unique, this event serves as a reminder that comprehensive resilience goes beyond mere code adherence.

### Integrated Fire Protection Planning

The growing demand for high-performance computing to support AI is reshaping data center design, power, and cooling. Data centers are expected to consume a growing share of US electricity as AI and digital services expand. As computing densities increase, liquid cooling is projected to become more widespread, and on-site generation and energy storage may be used to improve power reliability.Fire protection strategies must evolve with these systems. The most effective approach will integrate fire protection early into the design process, with input from other disciplines involved in the project, rather than relying on a single suppression technology or prescriptive solution. Testing and commissioning are equally important to confirm systems perform as intended. The core principles remain controlling ignition sources, early problem detection, limiting fire spread, and effective suppression, with the challenge lying in applying these fundamentals as technology advances.

stories.title: AI Data Centre Expansion Faces Power, Workforce Constraints

This growth is leading to significant infrastructure constraints that could challenge the industry's pace of expansion.
stories.content:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying demand for data centres, electricity, and skilled labour globally, according to technology leaders. This growth is leading to significant infrastructure constraints that could challenge the industry's pace of expansion.

Highlights

AI expansion drives immense demand for data centres, electricity, and skilled labour.

Mark Zuckerberg noted data centre construction requires millions of skilled trade jobs.

Elon Musk warned of a significant power shortfall for AI infrastructure next year.

Tesla is building power generation alongside its data centres to meet electricity needs.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing demand for data centres and the electricity and skilled workforce needed to support them, with technology leaders warning that infrastructure constraints could become a major challenge for the industry.Speaking virtually at a G20 technology ministers' meeting, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg stated that the scale of data centre construction is creating immense demand for skilled workers. He noted that the buildout would require hundreds of thousands and potentially millions of jobs in skilled trades.Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk highlighted the growing electricity requirements of AI infrastructure, describing a potential power shortfall as a near-term challenge for data centre expansion. Musk added that his company is building power generation alongside its data centres to address these needs, predicting a significant power shortfall next year.

Infrastructure Challenges for AI Compute

The infrastructure buildout for increasingly compute-intensive AI systems is putting greater pressure on electricity generation and the availability of skilled workers needed to construct and operate large-scale facilities. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis also commented on the economic impact of increasingly capable AI systems, emphasising the need for responsible development.Access to reliable power and infrastructure talent are emerging as critical factors in determining the pace at which data centre capacity can expand, moving beyond traditional concerns such as chip and computing capacity.

stories.title: Data Centers Rarely Reuse Cooling Water Due to Economic Trade-offs
stories.summary: Most data centers do not reuse cooling water on-site, primarily due to the nature of evaporative cooling systems and the economic and operational complexities of treatment. This practice raises concerns about local water consumption, especially as facilities scale.
stories.content:
Most data centers do not reuse cooling water on-site, primarily due to the nature of evaporative cooling systems and the economic and operational complexities of treatment. This practice raises concerns about local water consumption, especially as facilities scale.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

A 100 MW data center consumes about 2.5 billion litres of water annually, similar to 5,000 homes.

Evaporative cooling releases most water as vapor; recapturing it for reuse is inefficient.

Residual blowdown water requires costly treatment to remove concentrated minerals for reuse.

Closed-loop systems and blowdown treatment offer water reduction but involve higher costs and complexity.

Despite public concern over data center water consumption, most facilities currently do not reuse cooling water on-site. A 100 MW data center can consume approximately 2.5 billion litres of water annually, comparable to the usage of 5,000 or more homes.The primary reason for this limited reuse stems from the design of common direct evaporative cooling systems. These systems reject heat by releasing most water as vapor into the atmosphere, making on-site recapture inefficient as it would require reabsorbing the expelled heat.

Cooling System Dynamics and Water Use

Evaporative cooling is widely adopted due to its ability to remove large volumes of heat at relatively low cost and with less electricity consumption compared to alternative methods. After the evaporation process, 20% to 30% of the water remains as residual or "blowdown" water. This residual water contains concentrated dissolved minerals, which can lead to scaling and fouling if not periodically flushed from the system. Consequently, this blowdown water is typically treated as wastewater and discharged to municipal systems or in accordance with environmental regulations, rather than being reused directly for cooling without extensive treatment.

Pathways to Reduce Water Intake

While widespread on-site reuse is uncommon, data centers have several practical strategies to reduce potable water demand:

Closed-Loop or Hybrid Systems: Adopting closed-loop systems, such as chilled-water loops with dry coolers, circulates fluids through pipes and heat exchangers, leading to near-total fluid reuse. However, these systems often involve higher capital costs, larger footprints, and increased electricity consumption in various climates.

Blowdown Treatment: Operators can treat residual water using methods like softening, filtration, or reverse osmosis to remove minerals. While the technology exists, the added cost and operational complexity of these treatment systems have deterred many data centers from investing.

Graywater Repurposing: Residual water can be treated and repurposed for non-potable uses like irrigation or toilet flushing, depending on local codes, storage capacity, and consistent on-site demand.

Future Outlook for Water Recycling

Currently, the economics for widespread water reuse are not compelling in most markets. The alternatives to evaporative cooling are expensive, and treating residual water adds significant cost and operational complexity. This situation could change with rising water prices, increased scarcity, or stricter regulations that might include direct reuse mandates, water budgets, or discharge limits. For now, most water entering evaporative systems is not reused on-site but returns to the natural watershed as vapor through the cycle of evaporation and precipitation.

stories.title: Firmus commits US$300 million to SUBCO's APX East trans-Pacific cable
stories.summary: Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus Technologies is investing approximately US$300 million in SUBCO's planned APX East subsea cable, locking in up to 150Tbps of dedicated capacity between Australia and the United States for 25 years. The commitment positions Firmus as a cornerstone customer of the direct trans-Pacific system.
stories.why_it_matters: An AI infrastructure player anchoring a subsea cable with a quarter-century capacity commitment shows how compute companies are moving upstream to secure network supply as a competitive moat. The deal also de-risks financing for APX East, improving the odds that Australia gains a new direct US route independent of hyperscaler-built systems.
stories.content:
Firmus Technologies has agreed to invest approximately USD 300 million in SUBCO’s planned APX East submarine cable, securing up to 150Tbps of dedicated capacity between Australia and the US for 25 years. The agreement makes Firmus a cornerstone customer of APX East, which SUBCO is developing as a direct Australia-US system targeting Ready for Service in the fourth quarter of 2028.

The companies said the capacity will form an international connectivity layer for Firmus’s planned network of AI Factories in Australia, supporting the movement of data between its facilities and customers in the US and other international markets. While the deal is one of the more substantial commitments to international connectivity announced by an Australian data centre or AI infrastructure company, the USD 300 million investment and 150Tbps capacity are commitments under the agreement rather than capacity currently in service.

Firmus co-CEO and co-founder Tim Rosenfield said the company needed to consider connectivity alongside the development of its AI infrastructure. “Building the compute is only part of the challenge. We also need to reliably connect that infrastructure to the world,” Rosenfield said. “Securing up to 150 terabits per second of dedicated capacity gives us the scale and performance to connect Australian AI infrastructure directly with the United States.”

### Direct route to the US

APX East is being designed as an independent, direct trans-Pacific route between Australia and the US. SUBCO founder and co-CEO Bevan Slattery said the system was initially motivated partly by concerns about the resilience and capacity of existing international routes.

In a discussion released alongside the announcement, Slattery said existing routes were becoming increasingly “tired and overbuilt” and argued that new infrastructure could improve the resilience of Australia’s international connectivity.

A key feature of APX East is its planned express route. Slattery said improvements in subsea system efficiency had reduced power consumption per amplifier by about 20 percent, allowing the system to cover approximately 13,000 kilometres without additional power input and avoid a traditional landing in Hawaii.

The resulting route is intended to provide a lower-latency direct connection between Australia and the US, although the companies’ announcement is more focused on capacity and connectivity as opposed to positioning latency as a defining requirement for AI workloads.

Rosenfield said the cable represented an extension of Firmus’s approach to building its AI infrastructure. “We’re building a network of AI Factories across Australia. But building the compute is only part of the challenge. We also need to reliably connect that infrastructure to the world.”

SUBCO’s Slattery said the agreement reflected growing international connectivity requirements associated with AI infrastructure. “The connectivity requirements of AI are fundamentally reshaping demand patterns on international subsea routes,” he said.

### Building an Australian AI infrastructure network

Firmus is developing AI Factory projects in several Australian states, with its plans including facilities in Tasmania and South Australia as well as projects elsewhere in the country. The company has increasingly positioned its model as vertically integrated, spanning energy, data centre infrastructure, compute and connectivity.

Rosenfield said the APX East agreement was intended to provide a long-term international route for the output of those facilities. “This is a 25-year investment in Australia’s future,” he said. “AI is fast becoming one of Australia’s next major export industries, but that opportunity will only be realised if we invest in the infrastructure that underpins it.”

APX East is currently in development, with SUBCO targeting commercial service in Q4 2028. The system adds to the company’s existing portfolio of submarine cable projects, including INDIGO West, INDIGO Central and the Oman Australia Cable.

The agreement also gives Firmus a long-term commitment to international connectivity several years before its planned AI Factory network is expected to reach full scale, linking its Australian infrastructure strategy to the development timetable of a new trans-Pacific cable.

stories.title: AI Inference Demands Reshape Data Centre Infrastructure
stories.summary: Google's Anahita Mouro says the industry-wide shift from AI training to real-world inference workloads is fundamentally changing data center requirements, with new demands on power delivery, cooling, and operational resilience. The transition is expected to require gigawatt-scale facilities paired with dynamic infrastructure management.
stories.why_it_matters: When a hyperscaler of Google's scale reframes facility design around inference, it sets expectations that cascade through developers, equipment vendors, and utilities. Operators planning new APAC builds now face pressure to design for workload patterns and power densities that differ markedly from the training campuses of the past few years.
stories.content:
### Inference vs. Training Workloads

Mouro explained that AI training is typically a batch workload, allowing for checkpoints and restarts in case of failure, which is costly but not user-facing. In contrast, inference is a production, user-facing workload that requires low latency, high availability, and resilience under variable load, similar to critical web services. This distinction becomes even more pronounced with agentic AI systems, which involve multi-step workflows where the performance of the entire interaction depends on the tail latency of dependent actions.The growth in inference server spending, projected at around 42% annually through 2028, is roughly double that of training. This growth translates into a physical reality of deploying gigawatt-scale data centres. Hardware procurement is also splitting, with latest-generation graphics processing units (GPUs) for training and a more diverse mix of inference-optimised chips, older-generation GPUs, and purpose-built application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for serving.

### Infrastructure as a Pacing Factor

Power and cooling requirements are shifting from provisioning for constant, predictable loads to managing variable, bursty loads dynamically. Network infrastructure must also adapt to support dynamic load balancing. Mouro emphasised that infrastructure has become the pacing factor, with chip development outpacing the physical infrastructure that houses and powers them. Power availability, cooling capacity, and grid interconnection timelines have not accelerated at the same rate as silicon innovation.This disparity means that future infrastructure innovation will focus less on installing more powerful hardware and more on closing the gap between technological development and physical deployment through efficient facility design, dynamic power management, and smarter site selection.

### Operational Discipline and Digital Twins

The sheer pace and complexity of deployment present significant operational challenges. Hyperscale AI facilities integrate power systems, liquid cooling, networking fabrics, and thousands of accelerators, running dynamic workloads with varying power and thermal signatures. Mouro stressed that operational discipline is crucial to ensure reliability and consistency across diverse regional conditions.The growing role of digital twins and intelligent automation is emerging as a solution to manage this complexity. Digital twins can model power, thermal, and network behaviour before physical changes are made, enabling operators to predict and prevent incidents rather than reacting to them. This shift towards predictive operations, combined with robust operational playbooks, aims to maintain high reliability in increasingly complex environments.

### Talent Gap in Infrastructure

Mouro also highlighted the overlooked challenge of attracting and developing the talent required for AI infrastructure build-out. The industry faces a visibility problem, leading to a shortage of power systems engineers, thermal engineers, networking specialists, mechanical and civil engineers, software and operations professionals, as well as legal, safety, planning, environmental, and economic specialists. She argued that the skills developed in managing dense, variable, latency-sensitive systems at scale will be valuable for decades, making it a viable career path to invest in.

stories.title: AWS Builds 420 Tbps Subsea Cable for AI Infrastructure
stories.summary: Amazon Web Services is constructing a transpacific subsea cable with 420Tbps of capacity linking Japan to Washington state, with the system expected to enter service in 2029. The route is being engineered to handle traffic from distributed AI model training and edge computing workloads.
stories.why_it_matters: Hyperscalers building their own transpacific systems rather than leasing capacity signals that AI traffic growth is outpacing what consortium cables can deliver. Japan-US connectivity gains a major new route, while traditional wholesale carriers face losing their largest customers to self-owned infrastructure.
stories.content:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is constructing a 420 terabits per second (Tbps) subsea cable between Japan and Washington state, expected to be operational by 2029. This new transpacific route aims to bolster network capacity for bandwidth-intensive applications, particularly distributed artificial intelligence (AI) model training and edge computing. The project underscores the escalating demand for robust network infrastructure as hyperscalers expand their global computing footprint.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

AWS is building the 420 Tbps Sta’O’Nuk subsea cable from Japan to Washington state.

The cable, with 20 fiber pairs, is scheduled to enter service in 2029.

It will support bandwidth-intensive applications like distributed AI model training and edge computing.

Toptana Technologies is developing the Washington landing station, connecting to Seattle and Hillsboro.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is building the Sta’O’Nuk, a 420 terabits per second (Tbps) subsea cable system connecting Japan and Washington state, with an anticipated service entry in 2029. This initiative is designed to add a new transpacific route, supporting the expanding network infrastructure required by hyperscalers for their computing operations.The Sta’O’Nuk cable will feature 20 fiber pairs and is intended to handle bandwidth-intensive applications, including distributed large language model (LLM) training, financial transactions, edge computing, and video streaming. This project also establishes a new United States (US) landing point for AWS’s transpacific traffic, enhancing route diversity and network resilience.

New US Landing Point

Toptana Technologies is developing the Washington landing station in Ocean Shores, which will initially support four subsea cable systems and can expand to 16. This facility aims to connect international subsea cables with terrestrial fiber networks into major Pacific Northwest data center markets like Seattle and Hillsboro, Oregon, via a terrestrial backhaul network along the Interstate 5 corridor. Toptana Technologies, owned by the Quinault Indian Nation, is developing this as an Indigenous-owned telecommunications infrastructure facility, with Assured Communications serving as a strategic partner.

AI Demands Drive Network Expansion

The expansion of AI data center capacity across various regions is making the interconnecting networks a more significant component of infrastructure development. Jimmy Yu, Vice President at Dell’Oro Group, noted that hyperscalers were already primary consumers of subsea cables and capacity even before the recent surge in AI investments. The escalating demand for AI is expected to further drive the market for both terrestrial and submarine networks, according to Yu. He added that AWS’s choice of Washington underscores the importance of connecting subsea infrastructure to key data center markets, improving connectivity to a major US data center hub and adding network resilience.Ron Westfall, Vice President and Practice Lead for networking and infrastructure at HyperFrame Research, highlighted that large AI models can necessitate terabit-scale data transport between distributed training clusters and inference locations. As hyperscalers distribute computing resources across regions, network backhaul and interconnect capacity could become a bottleneck, similar to power availability. This creates a distinct infrastructure challenge, where power availability dictates data center location, while network capacity determines the effectiveness of connecting these facilities to other computing resources, cloud regions, and customers.

Geographic Diversity and Network Control

AWS states that Sta’O’Nuk will provide crucial geographic diversity between North America and Japan. Existing US landing sites for transpacific subsea cables are largely concentrated along the California and Oregon coasts. A new Washington landing point offers AWS an alternative path into the Pacific Northwest, reducing reliance on established corridors and connecting directly to Toptana’s planned terrestrial network. This integrated approach ensures that the international cable capacity can be efficiently moved from the coast to inland data center and network infrastructure.AWS’s global network already spans over 20 million kilometers of fiber. The Sta’O’Nuk project extends this strategy by adding another piece of physical infrastructure under direct AWS control. The cable will incorporate quantum-safe optical encryption at Layer 1 and be armored and buried in vulnerable areas, including depths up to 1,500 meters, to mitigate common causes of cable cuts such as fishing activities and dragged anchors.

stories.title: Fibre Connectivity: New Critical Infrastructure for AI Data Centres
stories.summary: Emtelle's Chief Commercial Officer Gavin Faulds argues that fibre must now be treated as critical infrastructure, alongside land, power, and water, in data centre planning. This shift is crucial for hyperscale facilities and AI workloads, which demand scalable and resilient physical connectivity.
stories.content:
### Strategic Shift for Connectivity

Historically, fibre has been treated as an infrastructure component that follows construction, with planning for it occurring after site acquisition, power allocation, and building design. This approach, according to Faulds, is no longer viable for modern hyperscale facilities driven by AI. Today's data centres are increasingly interconnected campuses, regional ecosystems, and global cloud platforms, with AI training clusters spanning multiple data halls and generating unprecedented east-west traffic.Retrofitting physical connectivity infrastructure in operational facilities is complex, costly, and introduces significant operational risk. Upgrading servers or cooling systems is more straightforward than re-routing ducts, adding fibre pathways, or revising access points in environments where uptime is paramount. Consequently, fibre planning needs to occur much earlier in the development process.

### Designing for AI Workloads and Future Flexibility

Operators must ask challenging questions about connectivity during initial planning stages, similar to how power requirements are assessed. These include whether a campus can double in size without major civil works, if sufficient route diversity is designed into the network, and if current duct infrastructure and fibre pathways will support future AI workloads.Planning for flexibility is as important as planning for capacity, given the unknowns in future AI infrastructure, compute densities, and optical technologies. This involves considering routes, ducts, and connection points that allow for future capacity additions with minimal disruption. Organisations that integrate fibre planning early will be better positioned to expand quickly, respond to customer demand, and avoid the substantial costs associated with rebuilding infrastructure not designed for evolution.The next generation of data centres will not only be constrained by power availability but also by the quality, resilience, and scalability of the connectivity linking buildings, campuses, cloud platforms, and customers. Fibre is therefore crucial for retaining future flexibility, reducing retrofit risk, and enabling operators to meet changing capacity requirements.

stories.title: China 15 years behind in top chipmaking tools, says ASML supplier
stories.summary: A supplier to lithography giant ASML estimates that China lags roughly 15 years behind the frontier in advanced chipmaking equipment. These tools are central to US export controls aimed at preventing China from producing or obtaining top-tier AI chips.
stories.why_it_matters: The assessment suggests Washington's export restrictions are having a durable effect, shaping where advanced AI compute can be built and operated for years to come. For APAC data center markets, it reinforces a bifurcated landscape in which China's AI infrastructure develops on a separate hardware track from the rest of the region.
stories.content:
Such tools are key targets of US efforts to block the country from acquiring top-flight AI chips

[BERLIN] China is about a decade and a half behind in developing cutting-edge chipmaking tools, according to a top executive at Germany’s Zeiss Group, a key supplier in the global semiconductor industry.

It is a “reasonable assumption” that Beijing will need 15 years to develop extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography machines, Frank Rohmund, who leads the semiconductor division at Zeiss, said on Bloomberg TV, while noting that the country’s progress is hard to quantify.

Chipmaking technology is a key target of US efforts to prevent China from acquiring top-flight artificial intelligence chips as the two biggest economies compete to develop cutting-edge models.

The US bars Zeiss shareholder ASML from shipping its most advanced machines to the country, while Beijing is pouring money into its domestic semiconductor sector in a bid for self-sufficiency.

Zeiss is the exclusive supplier of optics used in ASML’s EUV machines, and the Dutch company is the world’s only manufacturer of such equipment.

EUV technology is essential for producing the most advanced chips used in Nvidia’s AI accelerators.

Rohmund’s estimate comes after UBS analysts led by Francois-Xavier Bouvignies wrote this week that China is likely at least a decade away from developing domestic EUV technology.

China is one of ASML’s top markets for the previous generation of chipmaking machines that use deep ultraviolet, or DUV, technology. The US also requires export licenses for several of the Dutch company’s more sophisticated immersion DUV models.

Any plan to expand export controls to include legacy DUV machines would be bad for business, according to Rohmund.

SEE ALSO

“We don’t believe in the positive impact of these export restrictions because it accelerates innovation in China,” he said.

China has made strides in producing immersion DUV lithography tools. A Shanghai-based company is making such equipment, *The Information* reported in July, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter. 

Beijing has been working on such technology for decades, according to Rohmund. “It doesn’t really come as a surprise and now we need to see how capable these tools really are,” he said of reports of recent advances.

“We are still way ahead,” he added.

Zeiss says its components are used to produce around 80 per cent of the world’s chips. ASML bought a minority stake in the Oberkochen, Germany-based company’s semiconductor division in 2017 for 1 billion euros (US$1.2 billion).

To accommodate AI-driven demand, Zeiss has expanded its Oberkochen headquarters to add production. It is also constructing a factory on another site. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Hitachi Vantara posts 32% Asia Pacific revenue growth on AI-driven storage refresh
stories.summary: Asia Pacific buyers are replacing ageing storage to ready data systems for AI, helping Hitachi Vantara lift product revenue 52% in the region.
stories.content:
![Hitachi Vantara posts 32% Asia Pacific revenue growth](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/09/03/wendy-koh_pic-2-story-318156.webp) 

# Hitachi Vantara posts 32% Asia Pacific revenue growth

Thu, 3rd Sep 2026 (Today)
![Karen Joy Bacudo](<https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyMSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--019183c634a09650fab653c6e35bf96cd3b99fba/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/images%20(22)%201.webp>) 

Hitachi Vantara reported 32% year-on-year revenue growth across Asia Pacific in its first quarter, with product revenue in the region up 52%.

Storage revenue in Asia Pacific increased 61%, while block portfolio revenue rose 58%. Within that, high-end storage revenue grew 48% and midrange storage revenue increased 65%.

The regional result was led by sharp gains in several markets. Revenue in Korea rose 185% year on year, mainland China grew 112%, Australia and New Zealand increased 30%, and ASEAN, including Singapore, was up 22%.

Hitachi Vantara attributed the growth to demand for its Virtual Storage Platform One portfolio, known as VSP One, as customers updated core infrastructure and prepared data environments for broader AI use.

The figures point to continued spending on storage and related systems as businesses in the region manage larger, more complex data estates. Companies are also weighing cyber resilience and operational efficiency as they review older infrastructure.

Industry data cited by Hitachi Vantara showed the broader market has also expanded. According to IDC, worldwide external OEM enterprise storage systems revenue increased 22.7% year on year in the first three months of 2026, driven by AI infrastructure demand and delayed refresh cycles.

The company said its Asia Pacific figures cover ASEAN, including Singapore, Australia and New Zealand, mainland China, Hong Kong, India, Korea and Taiwan, and exclude Japan.

### Storage demand

Recent product strategy has focused on unifying block, file and object data on a single platform. The approach is intended to help customers manage data across on-premises and cloud environments with fewer operational silos.

VSP One Block High End is aimed at mission-critical applications, mainframe systems and AI workloads. The system is designed to let organisations consolidate open systems and mainframe workloads on one platform.

Hitachi Vantara also said VSP 360 offers centralised management and operational visibility across storage environments. Product specifications highlighted by the company included support for up to 50 million input/output operations per second, availability of eight nines and a 4:1 data reduction guarantee.

The business case for such systems is shifting as corporate AI projects move from model testing to preparing and governing the data those models use. That has increased attention on older transactional and mainframe environments that still hold critical records in sectors such as financial services, telecommunications, manufacturing, healthcare and government.

Wendy Koh, Vice President and General Manager, Asia Pacific, Hitachi Vantara, commented on the regional results.

"The momentum we're seeing across Asia Pacific reflects a common challenge facing organisations today: how to modernise critical infrastructure while preparing for an AI-driven future," said Wendy Koh, Vice President and General Manager, Asia Pacific, Hitachi Vantara. "Organisations are looking for ways to simplify increasingly complex data environments while improving resilience, operational efficiency and business agility. Our first-quarter performance reflects the confidence customers place in Hitachi Vantara to help them address these challenges and create lasting value from their data."

### Market context

Analysts have increasingly linked storage spending to the practical demands created by AI deployments, especially when businesses want to connect new AI tools with long-established systems of record. That trend has supported investment not only in raw capacity but also in management tools, resilience features and consolidation projects.

Scott Sinclair, Practise Director, Infrastructure, Cloud & DevOps, Omdia, commented on the company's high-end storage offering.

"As organisations expand their use of AI while continuing to support mission-critical applications, they need storage infrastructure that can keep pace without making their environments harder to manage," said Scott Sinclair, Practise Director, Infrastructure, Cloud & DevOps, Omdia. "VSP One Block High End brings together the performance, resilience and scale these workloads demand in a unified platform, giving customers a practical path to modernise their data foundation while keeping complexity in check."

Separate research referenced by Hitachi Vantara suggested many technology leaders remain concerned about operational risk in more fragmented environments. It found that 55% of IT leaders said complexity makes breach detection harder, while 57% said data loss would be catastrophic to their business.

Those concerns help explain why storage suppliers are positioning infrastructure upgrades as both an AI enabler and a risk-management measure, particularly in regions where large enterprises are balancing cloud adoption with continued use of on-premises and mainframe systems.

In Asia Pacific, Hitachi Vantara's latest quarter suggests demand remains strongest where customers are willing to invest in replacing or consolidating older storage estates while preparing for heavier AI-related workloads.

stories.title: SK Hynix, other chip stocks climb as Asian equities advance

stories.content:
MSCI’s Asia-Pacific equities gauge rises 1.1%, rebounding from the prior session’s sell-off

ASIAN stocks rose and oil paused a three-day rally after US President Donald Trump played down the prospect of a prolonged conflict with Iran. The yen strengthened.

MSCI’s Asia-Pacific equities gauge advanced 1.1 per cent, rebounding from Wednesday’s sell-off. Chip-related stocks including Renesas Electronics and SK Hynix rose after Broadcom predicted a boom in artificial intelligence chip sales over the next two years.

Among the main moves in markets, S&P 500 futures were little changed as at 1.02 pm Tokyo time. Japan’s Topix rose 1 per cent, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.5 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was little changed and the Shanghai Composite rose 0.4 per cent.

Futures indicated a tepid open in Europe, while contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index edged up 0.2 per cent.

Attention in Asia was on the yen, which gained for a second session, strengthening to as much as 157.63 per US dollar. The currency’s spike left traders guessing about possible intervention by authorities.

Elsewhere in Japan, an auction of 30-year government bonds drew strong demand. The 30-year yield earlier fell 10 basis points to 4.065 per cent.

Adding to the positive tone, Brent halted a three-day rally, trading a touch lower at around US$95.40 a barrel. Oil slipped after Trump said renewed attacks on Iran would likely be short-lived and reiterated his claim that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz.

The pullback in crude eased pressure on Treasuries, which held gains from the previous session.

The brighter tone followed a cautious start to September, when global bond yields surged as renewed fighting in Iran drove oil higher, fuelling inflation concerns and bets on a US Federal Reserve interest rate hike in September.

stories.title: Opinion: Southeast Asia's chance to become a strategic hub for the AI global supply chain
stories.summary: There is a global competition to develop artificial intelligence (AI). However, AI development goes beyond software and algorithms and is enabled by advanced hardware components, including semiconductor chips, hard drives, network devices, and other computing peripherals. All these are ultimately housed in data centers that make up cloud computing infrastructures.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Sept 3): There is a global competition to develop artificial intelligence (AI). However, AI development goes beyond software and algorithms and is enabled by advanced hardware components, including semiconductor chips, hard drives, network devices, and other computing peripherals. All these are ultimately housed in data centers that make up cloud computing infrastructures.

Given the complex manufacturing processes and globalisd production networks that drive intense competition to build and secure hardware, a reassessment of the global supply chain strategy is necessary. Traditionally, technology companies have prioritised low-cost locations for sourcing or manufacturing hardware components. In light of AI’s strategic importance, acute material shortages, and vulnerability to disruptions, companies must align supply chain strategies with overall business value chain objectives, with emphasis on resilience, security, and sustainability over cost reduction alone.

The AI hardware value chain encompasses multiple stages: research, design, development, manufacturing, and distribution. Table 1 details the component groups within each stage. To prevent delivery hiccups at each stage of the value chain, the supply chain requires a reliable, secure flow of raw materials and resources from upstream to downstream. As such, there is a growing need for proximity to tighten the supply chain and cluster activities for better coordination of end-to-end operations.

**Table 1. Stages of the AI hardware value chain and their principal component groups**

*Source: Compiled by the authors from industry sources.*

However, companies need to be cognisant that overconcentration of suppliers in co-location might create unintended risks, particularly energy, cyber, and physical security. For example, the recent Strait of Hormuz crisis caused an acute shortage not only of liquefied natural gas but also of helium, a critical gas in the photolithography process for integrated chip production, leading to a bottleneck in advanced chip production, especially for TSMC. In addition, service disruptions occurred across banking and other sectors after drones hit three of Amazon's data centre in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. In an unrelated case, Apple’s primary contract manufacturer, Foxconn, experienced a cyberattack in its North American facilities. These security issues amplify the impact of a single event and highlight the importance of a more carefully thought-out location-specific supply chain strategy.

Rather than focusing on a single location, an optimal sourcing strategy would be to limit geographical dispersion by nearshoring across countries within the same region. This regional spread is particularly important to ensure reliable and sustainable sourcing. It also offers alternative or multiple sourcing, enabling collaboration and competition whilst diversifying away from reliance on a single supplier and location.

Southeast Asia comprises 11 countries located between India and China. As a region, it is rising fast to become the fourth-largest economy globally, and a major driver of global economic growth. The region enjoys relative political stability and strong economic growth potential, and it promotes trade-openness policies, thereby mitigating geopolitical risks. Additionally, it is rapidly adopting digital technologies, with a young workforce and a relatively high literacy rate, essential for the labour-intensive, large-scale development of the manufacturing sector to progress along the value chain.

In light of the US-China trade conflict, which is driving the decoupling of the AI supply chain, Southeast Asia is emerging as a viable alternative or complementary source to a China-centric focus, offering a “China Plus One” strategy. Companies can maintain operations in China while concurrently expanding or relocating activities to Southeast Asia.

However, China Plus One is only the most immediate reason to look at Southeast Asia; the more durable reason is structural.

Strategically, Southeast Asia's diverse economic profile offers technology companies a critical opportunity to build a long-term competitive advantage. Historically, the region began developing its high-tech electronics manufacturing sector over half a century ago, driven by Singapore in the 1960s, Malaysia in the 1970s, and Thailand in the 1980s through foreign direct investment. The sector's maturity is due to strong multifaceted government support through trade policies, innovation funding, tax incentives, and other measures. Mature manufacturing operations are a critical advantage, lowering barriers to entry during sourcing shifts.

Singapore has developed a comprehensive semiconductor ecosystem with a comparatively strong focus on semiconductor research, chip design, and front-end wafer fabrication. On the other hand, Malaysia has an established electronics and semiconductor manufacturing base, and excels primarily in back-end assembly, test, and packaging. Thailand has developed into a global manufacturing hub for hard disk drives and the region's base for printed circuit boards. Meanwhile, Vietnam has benefitted significantly from the “China Plus One” strategy, owing to its proximity to China and the spillovers from the US-China trade conflict. For instance, OpenAI’s decision to produce its consumer hardware in Vietnam evidences its rapid evolution into a hub for manufacturing consumer electronics and computer components. Indonesia is leveraging its abundant natural resources, such as energy, water, and land, and aims to become the region’s data centre hub. The Philippines, meanwhile, is catching up with its version of AI Silicon Valley through the US-backed Pax Silica project.

**Table 2 summarises these country positions across the region.**

Southeast Asia’s rise in strategic importance is not episodic. Its AI supply chain is demand-driven, catering not only to the global market but also to rapidly rising domestic consumption. Thus, it is more systemic and scalable than if it were supply-driven. According to McKinsey & Co, Southeast Asia's AI adoption momentum surpasses the global average. What drives this momentum is the growing embedding of AI by enterprises operating in Southeast Asia. It will then spur domestic innovation and investment in AI and cloud services, and in turn, generate demand for co-located data centres. Having AI’s hardware supply in strategic proximity can easily fulfill this demand.

This is what gives the region a credible claim to becoming a strategic hub in the global AI supply chain.

The next article will dive deeper into Southeast Asia as a strategic hub for the global AI supply chain in the coming decade.

*Dr Andrei OJ Kwok is associate professor at Monash University Malaysia and Dr Neale O’ Connor is associate professor at LaTrobe University, Australia.*

stories.summary: SEOUL (Sept 3): Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) has proposed Samsung Electronics pay 20 trillion won (US$15 billion) in advance for power through to 2031 to help fund the expansion of its grid, the Chosun Ilbo reported on Thursday.

SEOUL (Sept 3): Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) has proposed Samsung Electronics pay 20 trillion won (US$15 billion) in advance for power through to 2031 to help fund the expansion of its grid, the *Chosun Ilbo* reported on Thursday.

It has also proposed that SK Hynix pay five trillion won in advance, the newspaper said, citing an internal KEPCO document.

State-run KEPCO, South Korea's main utility, said in a statement it had suggested an advance payment scheme to major power users including Samsung and SK Hynix, but that participation, interest rates, payment amounts and payment periods had not been finalised.

Samsung and SK Hynix declined to comment.

KEPCO said the proposed arrangement was intended to help meet rising investment needs from semiconductor and AI data centre projects, while providing companies with more certainty over timely power supply for new factories.

The utility would use the funds to build transmission and substation networks for chip fabs, while paying the companies interest above the yield on two-year Korean government bonds, according to the *Chosun* report.

stories.title: Kerjaya Prospek bags first data centre contract worth RM858 mil
stories.summary: Bursa Malaysia-listed Kerjaya Prospek has secured an RM858 million contract that marks the construction firm's first project in the data center sector. The company described the award as its entry into a new business segment.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia's data center construction boom is pulling mainstream builders into the sector, diversifying a contractor pool that has been strained by rapid development in Johor and the Klang Valley. For investors, the contract size shows how significant data center work has become to the order books of mid-cap Malaysian construction firms.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 3): Kerjaya Prospek Group Bhd (KL:KERJAYA) said it has secured a contract worth RM858 million that marks the construction firm’s first-ever job related to data centres.

The contract involves mechanical, electrical and plumbing fit-out works for a data centre at Iskandar Puteri, Johor from an undisclosed developer, the company said in an exchange filing on Thursday. The project is slated for completion within eight months.

“We view this project as a strong starting point to establish our presence in the data centre space,” Kerjaya Prospek chief executive officer Tee Eng Tiong said in a statement.

Malaysia has seen an influx of investments in data centres amid rapidly rising demand for advanced computing and artificial intelligence. The country is now home to 187 facilities concentrated in Klang Valley and Johor, according to Baxtel, which researches data centres.

The win lifts Kerjaya Prospek’s new contracts for 2026 to RM3.2 billion. Outstanding jobs on hand, meanwhile, totalled a record RM5.9 billion.

“Beyond the immediate contribution to our order book, the project will further enhance our capabilities, execution track record and industry expertise, positioning us to pursue a broader range of opportunities within this high-growth sector,” Tee added.

Kerjaya Prospek is currently valued at 15 times trailing earnings, the lowest among its peers, according to AskEdge data. Gamuda Bhd (KL:GAMUDA) trades at 26 times, followed by Sunway Construction Group Bhd (KL:SUNCON) at 25 times and Binastra Corp Bhd (KL:BNASTRA) at 19 times.

All nine analysts covering the stock have 'buy' recommendations. The average 12-month target price stands at RM3.36.

Kerjaya Prospek’s shares were up nine sen or 3.13% at RM2.97, valuing the company at RM3.76 billion ahead of the contract announcement during the noon trading break.
